<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Evaluating whether to implement the vet-stop hook directly, enrich the bead with requirements, or close it as unworkable.

The no-code-turn skip would help Q&A and docs turns. Yet git-based detection is fragile: it misses reverted edits and may false-negative on beads-only changes. The efficiency review also treats full vet as intentional quality gate in one place and accidental waste in another.

An opt-in `STEPDOWN_VET_SKIP_NO_CODE` flag would preserve the strict quality gate by default. Git diff alone is too brittle; tracking file edits or limiting diff to source directories would be more reliable. Env scrubbing is likely low-value because vet output rarely leaks secrets.

A blanket env scrub would be noisy and destructive. Targeting only known secret patterns like TOKEN, KEY, or SECRET is much safer. Both features are optional and gated by environment variables.

Decided to implement both features directly. The no-code-turn skip will use an opt-in environment variable to bypass vet when no relevant code files are dirty versus HEAD. Secret scrubbing will also be gated by an optional env flag. Neither change alters the default strict quality gate.

Drafting a `hasCodeChanges` helper that runs `git status --porcelain` filtered to source paths like `src`, `tests`, `scripts`, and config files. A simpler alternative would check for modified `.ts`, `.json`, or `.toml` files outside `.beads` and `.specstory`. The core limitation remains: the hook cannot know what the agent changed during this specific turn, only the current dirty state.

Prior dirty source files will still trigger vet, preserving the quality gate. The skip path filter now covers `src/`, `tests/`, `scripts/`, config files, and `.cursor/hooks/`. A `scrubSecrets` helper is being drafted to redact env values from followup text when `STEPDOWN_VET_SCRUB_ENV` is enabled.

The scrub logic will scan `process.env` for values longer than eight characters and match against secret key patterns like `SECRET`, `TOKEN`, `PASSWORD`, and `AUTH`, replacing each match with `[scrubbed:${key}]`. The next step is to check for existing `vet-stop` tests.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
No existing tests cover the vet-stop hook.

The hook runs `await main()` at the top level, making direct import difficult. I am weighing whether to split out pure helpers into a library file or keep the file intact and test via subprocess.

I will guard `main()` with `import.meta.main` so the hook can be imported and tested. I plan to add env-gated skip and secret scrubbing to `vet-stop.ts`, plus a small test file. I also want to verify whether custom-hooks or stepdown would flag the hooks file.

I will use two environment flags: `STEPDOWN_VET_SKIP_NO_CODE` to bypass vet when no code is dirty, and `STEPDOWN_VET_SCRUB_ENV` to scrub secrets from followup messages. Secrets will be scrubbed only when their value length is at least eight characters. The hook will fail-open if git status cannot be determined. I am now drafting the implementation in `vet-stop.ts`.

The implementation now defines `SCRUB_ENV` and a list of relevant code paths and filenames. When `SKIP_NO_CODE` is set, the hook returns early if no relevant code changes were detected. I am also beginning the `buildFollowup` helper.

I am implementing `hasRelevantCodeChanges` to run `git status --porcelain -z` and parse the resulting output. This will detect relevant code changes by scanning for modified or added files under the configured path prefixes.

The `hasRelevantCodeChanges` helper now parses null-separated git status entries. It skips the first three characters of each entry to extract the path, converts backslashes to forward slashes, and checks whether the path matches the configured code prefixes. If git status fails or returns non-zero, the function defaults to returning true so the vet still runs.

I realized splitting null-separated git status output is fragile because renames interleave entries. I will switch to non-z porcelain output and parse lines directly. A `linePath` helper will extract paths by stripping the first three characters and resolving `old -> new` renames. It will also handle quoted paths containing spaces.

I am defining `isCodePath` to match root-level config files and code paths under the configured prefixes. Root files like `package.json` will be matched by name alone.

The `isCodePath` helper now explicitly checks root-level config files such as `package.json` and `tsconfig.json` against a dedicated set. The scrub logic will be exported for unit testing. I am proceeding with implementation and adding tests, since the win is clear and the scope remains small.

I will add `tests/vet-stop.test.ts`. I need to check whether `custom-hooks`'s `fix` command might reorder `.cursor/hooks/vet-stop.ts`, since it currently places `main` before helper functions. I confirmed that skipping via `SKIP_NO_CODE` suppresses the followup emission. The scrub logic will be applied inside `buildFollowup` so existing fence sanitization continues to work.

I decided to scrub environment secrets from the entire assembled followup message rather than from individual parts. This ensures any secret embedded in the header or body is redacted. I am now writing the `scrubEnvSecrets` helper.

I will pass environment variables as parameters to `scrubEnvSecrets` and `shouldSkipNoCode` instead of reading `process.env` directly. This keeps the helpers pure and makes them easy to test without mutating global state.

I will update the bead with a description and acceptance criteria before closing it as completed. The header comment will document the new environment variables.
